description: Two years in to her leadership, Badenoch continues to take the Tories ever-rightwards, into comfort-zone Conservatism What happens to a political leader who is too sure of themself? Sometimes, huge confidence is a very useful, self-fulfilling quality: persuading party colleagues, activists, donors and voters that more can be achieved than is usually thought possible. Such utter conviction can keep everyone believing while the actual practicalities of a political project are worked out. The politician may be revealed as disastrously complacent and lacking in judgment, having delusions of grandeur, or being fundamentally in denial. description: It is getting ever harder for Eurosceptics to deny that it was an economic and strategic blunder for Britain to leave the single market The EU is a constantly evolving institution. The rules keep changing and, since Britain is destined by geography to want a close economic relationship with the bloc, there will always be something to negotiate in Brussels. Most of those discussions over the past two years have been uncontroversial, except in the eyes of dogmatic Eurosceptics. That doesn’t mean the talks have been easy. They never are with a club of 27 nations. But later this month, at a summit with the EU commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, Andy Burnham is expected to complete a treaty covering closer cooperation in a wide range of areas, including elimination of customs barriers to agricultural goods, a youth-mobility programme and integration with the EU’s carbon emissions trading scheme.

title: World leaders who sparred with Trump express relief mixed with caution at midterms
author: JILL LAWLESS and ROB GILLIES (Associated Press)
description: LONDON (AP) — World leaders who have sparred with the "America first" President Donald Trump greeted the rout of his Republican Party in the U.S. midterm elections with a measure of relief Wednesday, allowing themselves to hope for a less combative U.S. foreign policy. description: Readers respond to an article by Andy Burnham in which he says that people today can’t be held personally liable for the country’s historical wrongs In his opinion piece ( 30 October ), Andy Burnham argues that British people today cannot be held liable for historical wrongs “in which they played no personal part”. On one level, he is right. But he confuses two very different things: personal liability and the continuing responsibility of the state. When slavery was abolished in the British empire in 1833, the government borrowed £20m – an extraordinary sum then – to compensate enslavers for the loss of their supposed property. Some 40,000 claims were made. The British taxpayer carried the cost, and the resulting public debt was not finally cleared until 2015.

title: On Brexit, Andy Burnham could do worse than follow the lead of Pericles | Letter
author: Guardian Staff
categories: Brexit | Economic policy | Politics | UK news | Office for Budget Responsibility | Andy Burnham | Business | Economics
description: The Athenian led the people, he didn’t follow them, writes Prof Costas Milas Your editorial ( The Guardian view on a changing Brexit debate: Kemi Badenoch is trapped in denial, 29 October ) notes that when it comes to Brexit, Andy Burnham appears to be following the voters. This, in my humble opinion, is a problem. Thucydides noted about Pericles, the Athenian statesman, that “it was he who led them [the people], rather than they who led him”. It was arguably the constant and thoughtful guidance of Pericles to his fellow Athenian citizens that made Athens the dominant political and economic power, respected by its friends and enemies alike. Burnham needs to take the lead and show his cards on what type of relationship he wants to pursue with our European partners. To do so, he could start by asking the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) to produce an independent and authoritative analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of the different types of closer relationship with the EU.

To reassure parents, teachers of the public secondary school gave a tour of the facilities, which they had spent the summer break fortifying. Metal fences now towered over the schoolyard’s walls and the door had been replaced by a sturdy metal gate. The British Social Attitudes survey , the nation’s long-running annual pulse-taker, finds growing job dissatisfaction in its report, published today. People complain of a lack of flexibility in working hours, a lack of career advancement – and, of course, a lack of pay rises. Who is surprised?
